title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that measured the marginal effect of inserting an executable emulator validator and a bounded repair policy into an intent→configuration pipeline driven by a single LLM. Using a shared-generation paired design, we produced one candidate per task (gpt-5-mini; model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated that candidate both as a baseline (LLM-only suggestion) and as guarded (executable validator ± one repair). Task bank: N = 120 intent→configuration tasks (40 each: edge, core, leaf–spine). Outcomes (binary pass/fail defined by the archived scorer/validator fields): baseline successes = 120/120; guarded successes = 120/120; paired contingency: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces record repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We (1) present the preregistered protocol and a compact, formal scoring rule mapping archived scorer/validator fields to the binary outcome; (2) add a concise nearest-work comparison matrix that contrasts our shared-generation paired design with related closed-loop NetOps evaluations; and (3) provide condensed provenance and reproducibility guidance pointing to the archived execution and analysis artifacts. We interpret the degenerate ceiling result and give prescriptive design adjustments for future confirmatory runs intended to exercise repair behavior.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) promise to convert operator intent into actionable network configurations. However, syntactically correct command sequences can still violate workflow invariants (sequence, availability, make-before-break) and produce semantic failures only visible during stateful execution. Prior work therefore proposes integrating verification, emulation, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. To isolate the incremental effect of such validators and bounded repairs we preregistered and executed a paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that fixes the generator output per task and measures whether an executable validator plus at-most-one repair changes pass/fail outcomes for identical candidates. The central confirmatory question is: Does adding an executable emulator validator and a bounded repair step reduce emulator-observed semantic failures compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow when the same generator output is evaluated under both conditions? Our contribution is primarily methodological: a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design that isolates validator/repair marginal effects, a compact formalization of the binary scoring rule used for confirmatory inference, a concise nearest-work comparison, and concrete recommendations for future study designs when generators produce too few invalid candidates.
sections.related_work: Two strands frame our study. First, executable closed-loop benchmarks and verification tools demonstrate that syntax-level correctness is insufficient: closed-loop emulation and formal verification reveal sequencing and stateful errors (make-before-break, group-availability violations) that text-only checks miss. Representative verified sources include NetConfArena (arXiv:2608.23179) and other executable-benchmark efforts (arXiv:2604.22513). Second, a growing literature advocates tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails—veto layers, generate→validate→repair loops, translation-to-formal-model and digital twins—to reduce operational risk (see surveys/position papers in the archived bibliography). Those works typically evaluate generator variability and verification jointly; comparatively few experiments isolate validator marginal effects under identical generator outputs. Table 1 (nearest-work comparison) summarizes the closest verified studies and marks where our shared-generation paired design differs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and overall design. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) and executed under the stated paired-binary confirmatory plan. Task bank: N = 120 paired tasks partitioned into three deterministic topology classes (40 tasks each). Execution contract used a shared-initial-candidate stage: for each task a single generator output (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini) was created and evaluated under baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline invoked an executable emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that enforces structured workflow policies derived from task payloads. The preregistered primary test was exact two-sided McNemar on paired pass/fail labels; a bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) accompanied the estimate.

Compact provenance and reproducibility paragraph. All primary execution and analysis artifacts required to reproduce the reported accounting are archived and available in the run bundle. Representative artifact names (archived in the execution manifest) include: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl (task payloads and difficulty metadata), execution/model_configuration.json, execution/responses/*, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap parameters and seed). The run completed with planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, model_calls_used = 120, and no technical exclusions. Checksums and the full artifact manifest are recorded in the archived execution manifest; the immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 recorded in the Disclosure Statement). This paragraph replaces the longer provenance inventory previously included in-line.

Formal binary scoring rule (compact, unambiguous). For each episode the archived scorer/validator produced structured fields. We mapped those fields to a binary outcome (Success = 1; Failure = 0) as follows (the decision rule used by the confirmatory analysis and implemented in the archived analysis pipeline):
- Success iff (scorer.scoring_status == "COMPLETED") AND (scorer.scoring_rule == "full_intent_constraint_validation") AND (scorer.score == 1) AND (validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true) AND (validator_trace.violation_count == 0).
- Otherwise Failure. Tie-breaks: episodes with scoring_status != "COMPLETED" would be excluded per preregistered technical-exclusion rules; none occurred in this run. This mapping is deterministic and applied to both baseline and guarded episodes before paired McNemar analysis.

Concrete archival example (pass). Execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (archived) illustrates a pass under the above rule: scorer.scoring_status = "COMPLETED"; scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation"; score = 1; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.violation_count = 0; normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer. No archived failing episodes exist in this run (see Results), so a concrete fail example cannot be drawn from the bundle.
sections.results:
Primary outcome and contingency. The run produced a single shared initial candidate per pair (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 120). Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 120/120; guarded successes = 120/120 (success rates 1.00 each). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces: repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; hence no repair_provider_trace artifacts were generated.

Per-topology counts (explicit). The deterministic partition produced 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology paired outcomes (from archived scoring artifacts): Edge: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Core: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Leaf–spine: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40. These per-topology counts are present in execution/scoring/* and analysis/condition_summary.csv.

Diagnostics and reconciliation. Representative scoring artifacts (e.g., task-000001) show parsed_command_count equals required_command_count in the task payload and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero exclusions. analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms provider-call audits and pair accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cache_miss_count = 120, cross-condition cache reuse = false). These artifacts underpin the confirmatory statistics reported above.
sections.discussion:
Interpreting the ceiling result. The shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by removing generator variance. This design trades generator variability for internal-control strength: if the generator rarely produces invalid candidates for the selected task bank and prompt, the validator will be idle and repair will never be invoked. That is exactly what the archived run demonstrates: every shared initial candidate satisfied the emulator policy checks, producing a degenerate contingency table (n_11 = 120). The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI are statistical expressions of this ceiling and are expected under the preregistered analysis when discordant pairs are absent.

Design lessons and prescriptive adjustments. To produce informative confirmatory tests about repair utility, a future preregistered run should deliberately increase the incidence of generator-induced violations while preserving controlled comparisons. Specific, artifact-grounded recommendations (derivable from task_manifest difficulty fields) are: (1) allow independent generation per condition for a prespecified subset so generator sampling variability can produce discordant outcomes; (2) concentrate confirmation power on tasks with high dependency_rule_count or difficulty level "very_hard" from the manifest; (3) prespecify controlled prompt perturbations (the preregistration included exploratory perturbations) on a subset to increase generator error rates; (4) consider an exploratory arm permitting >1 repair iteration to measure repair convergence and cost. The archived task_manifest.jsonl contains the difficulty metadata fields needed to operationalize these recommendations without changing the validator semantics.

Threats to validity (concise). Internal validity: strong (deterministic provisioning, full accounting, zero exclusions). Construct validity: limited by synthetic task payloads and the validator's policy encodings; not all vendor-specific failure modes are modeled. External validity: constrained by a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), a frozen prompt, and a synthetic deterministic task corpus. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline failure ≈ 0.40) were violated by the observed baseline = 0.00, making the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N = 120) holding generator outputs fixed to measure the marginal effect of an executable emulator validator and a bounded repair policy. All shared generator outputs passed the deterministic validator, producing concordant successes in baseline and guarded conditions (n_11 = 120), a paired-difference of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0), and a degenerate bootstrap CI. The primary scientific contribution is methodological: the artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and, combined with deterministic archival traces, supports reproducible failure analysis and transparent audit—even when the confirmatory test is degenerate. Archived artifacts and the compact formal scoring rule provided here enable targeted follow-ups that relax the shared-generation constraint, focus on high-difficulty tasks, or compare generator families to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
